articles.title: ‘Here, you can eat until you’re full’: Oleshky evacuees savour first proper meals in years
articles.summary: In a quiet hospital corridor in Kyiv, staff and volunteers push carts carrying steaming pots of chicken soup, bread and buckwheat porridge to patients recently evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky, in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region.
articles.content:
For most people, a bowl of soup is unremarkable. But for evacuees like Olha, who spent the last four-and-a-half years trapped in a war zone, the World Food Programme (WFP) meals are a feast.

“Our neighbours had eaten all the pigeons in the area, every last one,” the 50-year-old recalls. “I simply couldn’t understand how there could be hunger in the 21st century.”

Olha is one of hundreds of people evacuated from Oleshky in late October under a brief ceasefire who are now receiving medical check-ups and treatment in Kyiv hospitals. WFP and its Ukrainian partner, Iskra Dobra, were the first humanitarian responders to provide hot meals the moment they arrived.

“This is the first proper meal they have had in years,” said Richard Ragan, WFP Country Director in Ukraine.

Tweet URL

Food in short supply

When the war erupted in 2022, Oleshky was occupied – sitting on the frontline – and eventually cut off from humanitarian assistance. Olha and her husband, Serhii, were searched, interrogated and threatened. “By noon at the latest, everyone was indoors,” Serhii says.

Food grew scarce and prices soared, and a kilo of flour could cost as much as $12, evacuees say. In May, food deliveries ended altogether.

With no heating in their shell-damaged home, the family slept in three layers of clothes. Olha planted cucumbers, tomatoes and zucchini, rushing outside during brief lulls between attacks to tend them.

“It was terribly frightening. But what could we do? We had to eat,” she says.

Further down the corridor, 78-year-old Valentyna describes how she and her elderly neighbours made soup from wild plants. “There was no bread, no flour, nothing at all,” she says.

A full plate at last

“Until we reached the border, we were afraid anything could still happen,” Olha recalls. Then, suddenly, they were through. Along the road to Kyiv, people stood holding signs and Ukrainian flags to welcome them.

“We saw our people,” she says. “There was something so wonderful about their energy. A sense of peace.”

For Valentyna, the meals have been a revelation. “Here, you can eat until you’re full! I hadn’t seen so much food in years,” she says. “The borscht is absolutely delicious.”

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, WFP has provided the equivalent of 4.1 billion meals to Ukraine’s most vulnerable people. Every month, it reaches 357,000 people in frontline communities with emergency food and cash assistance, and some 200,000 students receive its daily school meals.

For the evacuees, the future remains uncertain, with homes they cannot return to and years of fear that will not simply disappear. But there is also the relief of being safe and, in a hospital room in Kyiv, having a hot meal waiting.

articles.personality_title: Evacuees from Oleshky enjoy their first hot meals after years of hunger
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Oleshky is a town in southern Ukraine that was occupied and cut off during the war starting in 2022. People living there faced extreme food shortages and danger for more than four years.

**What happened** – In late October, hundreds of people were evacuated from Oleshky to Kyiv hospitals. The World Food Programme (WFP) and its partner group, Iskra Dobra, brought hot meals like chicken soup, bread, and buckwheat porridge to these evacuees as soon as they arrived.

**Impact** – For many evacuees, these were the first proper meals they had in years. People like Olha and Valentyna described how they had to survive on wild plants or small, scarce food supplies during the occupation. Now, they can finally eat until they are full and enjoy fresh, hot food safely.

**What's next step** – The evacuees will continue to receive medical care and support in Kyiv. Meanwhile, WFP keeps delivering millions of meals every month to people affected by the war across Ukraine, helping those who remain in frontline areas and supporting schoolchildren with daily meals.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After years of hunger and hardship, evacuees from Oleshky are finally receiving warm, filling meals thanks to ongoing humanitarian aid.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les évacués d’Oleshky savourent leurs premiers repas chauds après des années de faim

**Prochaine étape** – Les évacués continueront de recevoir des soins médicaux et du soutien à Kyiv. Le PAM continue aussi de distribuer des millions de repas chaque mois aux personnes touchées par la guerre dans toute l’Ukraine, y compris aux enfants à l’école.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après des années de faim et d’épreuves, les évacués d’Oleshky reçoivent enfin des repas chauds et rassasiants grâce à l’aide humanitaire.
articles.personality_title_es: Los evacuados de Oleshky disfrutan sus primeras comidas calientes tras años de hambre
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Oleshky es una ciudad en el sur de Ucrania que estuvo ocupada y aislada durante la guerra desde 2022. Sus habitantes sufrieron graves escaseces de alimentos y peligro por más de cuatro años.

articles.title: While Russia tries to manipulate information, local civil society is teaching Armenians media literacy
articles.summary: With the proliferation of generative AI, disinformation and propaganda campaigns have become increasingly sophisticated. Armenia’s experience shows how they operate in a country moving away from its longstanding reliance on Russia.
articles.content:
This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Armenia is a small, landlocked country that has, for years, relied on Russian support in its long-term conflict with the neighboring oil-rich and authoritarian country, Azerbaijan. However, Armenia received a blow from Russia in 2022–2023, when it was not supported by Russian military forces during its conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

In September 2023, Azerbaijan launched a large-scale military offensive, expelled the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh, dissolved the government of the region, and incorporated the territory into Azerbaijan.

After this incident, when Russia did not support Armenia with its peacekeeping troops, likely because Vladimir Putin was already engaged in a full-scale invasion and war with Ukraine, Armenia visibly changed its attitude toward Russia.

Armenian Prime Minister ​Nikol Pashinyan started to work in earnest towards the goal of European Union ⁠membership for his South Caucasus country and increased diplomatic communication with the US.

He was re-elected on June 7, 2026. The election took place amid reports of Russian interference. Reuters, citing anonymous Western intelligence officials and documents, reported covert Russian efforts to undermine Pashinyan and support pro-Russian candidates, including through disinformation campaigns.

These elections showed how information warfare has expanded beyond social media. It now included fake news websites, AI-generated videos and material presented as reporting by reputable international media outlets.

According to the US-based disinformation monitoring organization NewsGuard, a Russia-linked campaign circulated 31 fabricated stories about Pashinyan in just one week. The stories accused him of election fraud and of trying to drag Armenia into a war with Russia.

Some of this material imitated international media outlets such as France 24 and Politico. Other stories impersonated Armenian news outlets, including Armenpress and CivilNet.

With the proliferation of generative AI, disinformation and propaganda campaigns have become increasingly sophisticated. Armenia’s experience shows how these campaigns operate in a country moving away from its longstanding reliance on Russia. At the same time, Armenian journalists and civil society are working hard to build media literacy to counter disinformation campaigns. This Digital Spark Spotlight interview is about one of these projects — “Verify First,” a platform where users can find reliable information.

Global Voices interviewed Armin Asryan, a member of the group of journalists, editors, and activists behind the media literacy project “Verify First,” which tackles Russian information manipulation and propaganda.

Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Armin Asryan (AA): We are a group of enthusiasts, operating through the ‘Socio Club’ — Social and Information NGO — and dedicated to driving positive change in Armenia’s information landscape.

We chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project because we were thrilled to see an opportunity to actively contribute to a healthier, more reliable information space on social networks. In response to the growing challenges of online misinformation, we developed a targeted initiative to produce six educational video reels focused on practical fact-checking techniques and media literacy, designed to equip everyday social media users with the tools to spot and counter misleading content.

GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

AA: The Armenian social media space is heavily impacted by disinformation, low-quality content, and online hostility. Every day, social media feeds reveal content that not only disappoints users but also generates widespread panic and fear.

These unreliable narratives actively erode public trust in vital institutions. Recognizing that this negative information environment harms societal well-being, we felt compelled to act. This critical challenge prompted us to undertake our project, aiming to equip users with the critical thinking and fact-checking tools needed to counter misleading content and foster a healthier digital community.

GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

AA: Our primary challenge was translating complex fact-checking concepts, such as lateral reading and AI artifact identification, into engaging, accessible content for ordinary social media users.

To achieve this, we focused on breaking down advanced media literacy techniques into simple, highly intuitive video reels. We designed our activities to ensure that even technologically non-advanced audiences could easily grasp and apply these verification tools. By stripping away heavy jargon and demonstrating practical, step-by-step digital hygiene habits, we empowered everyday viewers to independently spot disinformation, assess online sources critically, and navigate social media feeds with greater confidence and discernment.

GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

AA: This project was a mutual learning experience for our team and our community. Our target beneficiaries included adults aged 18 and older, with a strong focus on reaching audiences in regional villages. Witnessing their growth as they mastered practical fact-checking tools was deeply rewarding.

A key highlight of our impact was making this educational content fully accessible: we provided sign language translation for viewers with hearing impairments, ensuring that marginalized community members could benefit from our media literacy campaign. By bridging the digital and accessibility gaps, we helped foster a more informed, inclusive, and resilient public space across Armenia.

GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

AA: We learned. We learned about fact-checking. We learned to be a group. It was a rewarding process. And we became aware that even little actions can have a big effect. We are very excited.

GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

AA: It was interesting. Two groups of content creators worked on the project. One team was composed of professional journalists over 60 years old. Another team was composed of young and inspired professionals in content creation in their early 20s and 30s. It was fascinating to see how experience could go hand in hand with young minds and innovation. The combination of older-age experience with the enthusiasm of the young was the lesson we learned from this project.

GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

AA: The video reels we created are not a one-time event. We are going to use them during training and also share them with other civic actors. But we also think that we should build on this. Right now, we have some inspiring ideas that we want to bring to life. Let’s see what the future brings.

The project targets a broad public audience, including marginalized groups, and addresses a significant societal challenge with clear, detailed actions and outcomes.
articles.personality_title: Armenian group fights disinformation with media literacy education
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Armenia, a small country in the South Caucasus, has faced challenges from Russia’s shifting support and a large military offensive by Azerbaijan in 2023. This situation led to increased disinformation campaigns, especially during Armenia’s 2026 elections, where false stories and fake news spread widely.

**What happened** – A group of Armenian journalists and activists created a project called “Verify First” to help people spot false information online. Supported by an international grant program, they made easy-to-understand videos teaching practical fact-checking skills. Their goal is to help everyday social media users, including those in rural areas and people with hearing impairments, recognize and resist misleading news.

**Impact** – This project is important because it directly fights the spread of fake news fueled by advanced technologies like artificial intelligence. By making media literacy accessible to many, it helps people trust real information and reduces panic caused by false stories. It also brings together both young and experienced content creators, showing how teamwork can improve efforts to protect public information.

**What's next step** – The team plans to keep using the educational videos in future trainings and share them with other community groups. They are also developing new ideas to continue improving media literacy across Armenia.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Armenian journalists and activists are empowering citizens with simple tools to identify false information, strengthening the country’s ability to resist disinformation campaigns.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un groupe arménien lutte contre la désinformation grâce à l’éducation aux médias

**Resumen en una frase** – Periodistas y activistas armenios están dando a los ciudadanos herramientas simples para identificar información falsa, fortaleciendo la capacidad del país para resistir campañas de desinformación.

articles.title: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
articles.summary: The author of a major review on youth unemployment, due next week, acknowledges the change would mean some young people losing out on benefits.
articles.content:
Young people should have a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support, the author of a major review of youth unemployment has told the BBC.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister whose proposals on welfare and young people will be unveiled on Tuesday, said those who refuse to take up the help could lose their benefits.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Milburn called for a radical shift in government spending away from benefits for young people to measures that support them into work.

He claims spending on benefits for young people is 25 times as much as spending on employment support, and believes the ratio should shift to two to one.

That would mean significant cuts to benefit spending and significant extra taxpayers' cash for training, education or other forms of support.

Milburn said "the pendulum's swung far too far from the one to the other - £25 to one, and we can take everything to £2 to one".

He added: "To do that, we've got to invest, less in benefits, so we've got to be paying out less in benefits."

The former MP acknowledged that would mean some young people losing out on benefits, arguing the system should focus on helping people into work rather than keeping them dependent on welfare.
articles.reasoning: The article discusses a proposed legal guarantee for young people to have access to jobs, training, or employment support, which represents a significant policy shift aimed at reducing youth unemployment and promoting economic inclusion. This has broad societal impact by potentially improving the livelihoods and future prospects of many young people. The article provides sufficient context about the policy proposal, its rationale, and expected changes in government spending priorities, making it a substantive and meaningful story.
articles.personality_title: New plan aims to guarantee jobs or training for young people
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Youth unemployment is a big challenge in many countries. Some young people struggle to find work or training opportunities after school. Currently, the government spends much more money on benefits for young people than on programs that help them find jobs or training.

**What happened** – Alan Milburn, a former government minister, has proposed a new plan that would legally guarantee every young person a job, training, or employment support. This plan is set to be announced soon. Milburn suggests shifting government spending from benefits to programs that help young people get work or learn new skills. He also said young people who refuse this support might lose their benefits.

**Impact** – This plan could change how the government helps young people by focusing more on giving them chances to work or train rather than just giving money. It could help many young people build skills and find jobs, improving their future. The idea is to spend less on benefits and more on support, changing the balance from spending 25 times more on benefits to just twice as much.

**What's next step** – The government will review Milburn’s proposals and decide how to put them into action. If accepted, new laws and programs will be created to make sure young people get these guaranteed jobs or training opportunities. This might also mean some changes in how benefits are managed.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new government plan aims to guarantee young people a job, training, or support to help them succeed, shifting focus from benefits to opportunity.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau plan garantit un emploi ou une formation aux jeunes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le chômage des jeunes est un problème important dans de nombreux pays. Certains jeunes ont du mal à trouver un emploi ou une formation après l'école. Actuellement, le gouvernement dépense beaucoup plus d'argent pour les allocations que pour les programmes qui aident à trouver un emploi ou une formation.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Alan Milburn, un ancien ministre, a proposé un nouveau plan qui garantirait légalement à chaque jeune un emploi, une formation ou un accompagnement vers l'emploi. Ce plan doit être annoncé bientôt. Milburn propose de déplacer les dépenses publiques des allocations vers les programmes d'aide à l'emploi ou à la formation. Il a aussi dit que les jeunes qui refuseraient cette aide pourraient perdre leurs allocations.

**Impact** – Ce plan pourrait changer la manière dont le gouvernement aide les jeunes en se concentrant davantage sur les chances de travailler ou de se former plutôt que sur l'argent donné. Il pourrait aider beaucoup de jeunes à acquérir des compétences et à trouver un travail, améliorant ainsi leur avenir. L'idée est de réduire les dépenses d'allocations et d'augmenter le soutien, en passant d'une dépense 25 fois plus élevée pour les allocations à seulement deux fois plus.

**Étape suivante** – Le gouvernement va examiner les propositions de Milburn et décider comment les mettre en œuvre. Si elles sont acceptées, de nouvelles lois et programmes seront créés pour garantir aux jeunes ces emplois ou formations. Cela pourrait aussi changer la gestion des allocations.

**En résumé** – Un nouveau plan gouvernemental vise à garantir aux jeunes un emploi, une formation ou un soutien pour les aider à réussir, en privilégiant les opportunités aux allocations.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo plan garantiza empleo o formación para jóvenes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El desempleo juvenil es un problema importante en muchos países. Algunos jóvenes tienen dificultades para encontrar trabajo o formación después de la escuela. Actualmente, el gobierno gasta mucho más dinero en ayudas que en programas que ayudan a encontrar trabajo o formación.

**Qué pasó** – Alan Milburn, un exministro, propuso un nuevo plan que garantizaría por ley a cada joven un empleo, formación o apoyo para el empleo. Este plan será anunciado pronto. Milburn sugiere cambiar el gasto del gobierno de ayudas a programas que ayuden a los jóvenes a trabajar o aprender nuevas habilidades. También dijo que los jóvenes que rechacen esta ayuda podrían perder sus beneficios.

**Impacto** – Este plan podría cambiar la forma en que el gobierno ayuda a los jóvenes, enfocándose más en darles oportunidades para trabajar o formarse en lugar de solo dar dinero. Podría ayudar a muchos jóvenes a desarrollar habilidades y encontrar empleo, mejorando su futuro. La idea es gastar menos en ayudas y más en apoyo, cambiando el gasto de 25 veces más en ayudas a solo dos veces más.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno revisará las propuestas de Milburn y decidirá cómo implementarlas. Si se aprueban, se crearán nuevas leyes y programas para asegurar que los jóvenes tengan estas oportunidades garantizadas. Esto también podría cambiar la forma en que se manejan las ayudas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un nuevo plan gubernamental busca garantizar a los jóvenes empleo, formación o apoyo para ayudarlos a tener éxito, cambiando el enfoque de ayudas a oportunidades.
